At the final line, the guard spun around, flashlight raised, and asked, "Who's there?" she demanded, and somewhere in the dark, something answered with a low, patient hiss.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: A paper tissue left in a pocket breaks apart in the wash and scatters white shreds over every item in the load, which is why pockets are checked before washing.
story:
Elena's mother had been in the hospital for two weeks, which was how a thirteen-year-old came to be standing in the Blue Ribbon Laundromat on a Saturday morning with a garbage bag of clothes and no plan. Her dad had said "just throw it all in," but she had watched her mother separate loads her whole life, so she sorted on the folding table: darks in one pile, whites in another, towels in a third. The darks were the biggest pile, mostly her father's work shirts and her own black leggings, so she fed those into the machine first, dumped in the detergent, and pressed the button like she was launching a rocket.

Dillon was there too, because Dillon was always wherever something was happening. He had set up a folding stand by the door with a hand-lettered sign that said "DILLON'S FOLDING SERVICE, 50 CENTS AN ITEM" and he wanted, more than anything, a first customer. "You have a lot of items," he said hopefully, nodding at her garbage bag. "It would be feasible for you to hire me. Very feasible."

"I can fold my own clothes," Elena said, though she was not entirely sure that was true. She presumed the dryer would do most of the work anyway. Behind them, an old man was arguing with a machine that had eaten his quarter, and the air smelled like warm cotton and lemon soap, with a hum underneath it all like a hive of sleepy bees.

When she pulled the dark load out, every single piece was speckled with white. Her dad's navy shirt looked like it had been caught in a snowstorm. Dillon laughed so hard he knocked over his sign. Elena stood there holding a shredded mess and thinking, and then it clicked: nothing in the pile had been white going in, so the white had to come from inside the load. She dug through the speckled clothes, and down in one of her dad's jacket pockets she found the remains of a paper tissue, torn to pieces. One forgotten tissue, she realized, had broken apart in the wash and scattered shreds over everything in the whole load. That was why her mother always checked pockets. Nobody had ever told her that. She had to find it out the snowy-shirt way.

She picked every shred off by hand, which took forty minutes and made her fingertips numb, and Dillon folded six of her dad's shirts for a quarter because, as he put it, "first customer discount, plus I feel bad for you." Her conscience twinged a little about paying him with quarters from her dad's laundry fund, but she figured she had earned it. The second load was her whites, and before it went in, she went through every single pocket, one by one, even her own, and found a movie stub and a gum wrapper. That load came out clean, no shreds anywhere, and she stood in front of it for a second, proving her theory to herself.

At home she laid the speckled work shirt over the back of a chair, the one piece she hadn't been able to save. Her dad would notice, and she would have to explain it, and he would probably laugh and probably also be tired. She folded the clean shirts into a neat stack the way her mother did, collars lined up, and set them where they always went. Then she texted him: "Laundry done. Mostly."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Anna sat cross-legged on the living room floor with the remote balanced on her knee, waiting for the 100-metre final to start. Asma flopped onto the couch beside her, still holding the printout they'd made in the library that afternoon.

"Your dad's going to want the TV," Asma said.

"He's out. We have till seven." Anna turned the volume up.

On the screen, eight sprinters settled into their blocks. The commentator's voice conveyed urgency even in the seconds of silence before the gun, leaning on words like "rivalry" and "fastest field ever assembled." Then the crack, and the runners rose together and tore down the track.

It ended in a blur. Two of them crossed nearly as one, and the stadium noise swallowed everything else. The scoreboard flashed gold beside one name and silver beside another, then the times: 9.81 and 9.82.

"A hundredth of a second," Asma said. "That's less than a blink."

Anna rewound it and paused on the finish. The two bodies were almost a single shape. She looked at the medal table on Asma's printout, where the silver medalist now sat second in the rankings, one place behind the winner and one place ahead of the bronze.

"Look at this," Anna said, tapping the column of finishing positions. "First, second, third. Same as always."

"So?"

"So the second-place guy lost by a hundredth of a second today. But in the semi-final, the girl in third lost by almost a whole minute in the steeplechase. Both of them get the same thing on paper. A two and a three." Anna grabbed a pen from under the couch cushion and drew the medal table again, this time with the gaps stretched out to scale. First and second were a hair apart. Second and third were a canyon. "The ranking shows you the order. It doesn't show you the distance."

Asma leaned over the drawing. "So when my dad says our school is ranked second in the district, that could mean anything."

"It could mean barely second. It could mean almost first." Anna thought of the swim rankings posted outside the gym, her own name sitting ninth. She'd been treating it like a fact about how fast she was. Now she wanted the times themselves, not the order. "Can we get the actual results from the meet?"

"They're online. The commentary's pretty sparse, though, just splits and numbers."

"Numbers are all we need. Bring your laptop down here."

Asma climbed the stairs two at a time, and Anna pulled the coffee table closer and cleared a space for it beside the paused TV screen, where two runners still hung frozen, a hundredth of a second apart.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: In a double-blind trial, neither the participants nor the researchers know who is receiving the real treatment, so their expectations cannot sway the results.
story:
Caleb spread his science fair notebook across the library table and tapped the page where he had written, in big letters, "Which hot chocolate tastes best: brand X or the store brand?" Heather dropped into the chair across from him with three books about medieval history, because she was in the library's after-school history guild and had promised the librarian a report by Friday.

"Nobody will pick the cheap one honestly," she said, reading his plan. "They'll taste it, see the fancy label, and say the expensive one is better because they expect it to be better." Caleb argued with her for a minute, then stopped, because he remembered his brother swearing a headache medicine worked, and then swearing the same thing about a sugar pill their mom had given him by mistake. The medicine had not been the thing doing the work. The believing had been.

"So we hide the labels," Caleb said. "Cups marked A and B." Heather shook her head and pulled his notebook toward her. "Not enough. What if you pour the cups? You know which is which. You could hand somebody the good one with a bigger smile." She looked at him until he got it. He rewrote the plan so that Youcef, who was meeting them at the library in twenty minutes, would mix up the cups himself and write the code on a card he would seal in an envelope. Caleb wouldn't know, the tasters wouldn't know, and even the person handing out the samples wouldn't know. "My mom calls that a double-blind trial," Heather said. "Neither the testers nor the people running it know who's getting which." He asked her to paraphrase that in his notes, and she wrote it in one clean sentence.

The twist came at four o'clock, when Youcef arrived with the carton of brand X already opened. "I had to test it at home," he admitted. "So I know which cup is which by smell." That broke the whole plan, and for a moment Caleb thought the project was dead. Then he found the solution in the library's little kitchenette: paper cups with lids and straws. If nobody could smell the cocoa, Youcef's accidental knowledge couldn't leak out. Youcef poured, shuffled the cups in a random order, and sealed the answer card while Caleb turned his back to prove it.

Nine tasters from the history guild participated, mostly because Heather bribed them with the leftovers. Caleb called out "A or B?" and tallied votes. Seven out of nine picked the store brand. When Youcef slit open the envelope, the cheap cocoa had won, and Caleb felt a strange mix of triumph and disappointment, because his family had been paying extra for the fancy carton his whole life.

"Want to co-author the write-up?" he asked Heather, sliding the notebook toward her. She was already writing. "You owe me," she said. "My medieval guild report is due Friday, and I just spent my afternoon on chocolate." Youcef raised a lidded cup in a small toast. "To science," he said, and drank.

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: The brain keeps developing until about age 25, which makes young people more vulnerable to nicotine addiction than adults.
story:
Alexandra set her phone timer on the kitchen counter, next to a bowl of eggs and a half-eaten piece of toast. "Three minutes," she said to Libby, who was perched on a stool by the fridge. "That's how long I have to explain the whole thing to Mr. Nakamura tomorrow. Nicotine, the brain, why people can't stop."

Libby tapped the counter. "Pretend I'm him. Go." Alexandra took a breath. "Okay. Deep in your brain there's a reward pathway. It's the part that says, do that again, that was good. Food, friends, music, all of it runs through there. Nicotine sneaks into that system and cranks the dial way up. The brain gets used to the bigger signal, so normal things start to feel flat, and now you need the nicotine just to feel okay." She paused. "That's the addiction part. Wanting it isn't weakness. The pathway itself got rewired."

She had almost forgotten where she first learned it. Back in October, at Harry's cousin's birthday party, someone had passed around a slim silver vape on the back porch. Harry had held it out to her, casual, like offering gum. Alexandra had said no before she really knew why, and Harry had shrugged and said, "Probably smart. My sister says your brain keeps building until you're about twenty-five, so kids get hooked way easier than adults." She had stared at that little silver tube afterward, thinking about a brain still under construction, rooms being built inside her own head.

"Time," Libby announced, and Alexandra slumped. "Two minutes forty. I can do it faster." She paced between the counter and the table, trying the explanation again, and this time she tripped over the middle part. "The... the receptor thing. Ugh, cramming all this in one night might actually hinder me." Libby grinned. "That's a vocab word and you know it." Alexandra threw a dish towel at her, laughing, and the laugh was contagious; soon they were both wheezing while the eggs sat forgotten.

Then the kitchen door opened and Mr. Nakamura himself walked in, carrying a casserole dish, back early from the potluck next door because the landlord had called about a flooded basement. He blinked at the two girls, timer still ticking on the counter. "Practicing your presentation? I'm your audience tomorrow, you know." Alexandra went pink. Then Harry stepped in behind him, holding the silver vape from the party, and set it on the table. "It's a prop," he said quickly. "Empty. It's for your talk. I figured a real one would make everyone actually listen." Alexandra picked it up, turned it over in her hand, and looked at Mr. Nakamura. "Want the two-minute version now, or should I wait until I beat three minutes?"

"Beat the clock," he said, settling onto Libby's stool and folding his hands. "I'll count."

activity: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
knowledge_domain: to draw a street using one-point perspective with lines meeting at a vanishing point
fact: The lines that run back toward the vanishing point are called orthogonals, and in a street scene they include road edges, curbs and rooflines.
story:
Emilia pushed a fresh sheet of paper across the art room table so fast that her pencil rolled off the edge and bounced under the stool. Today Ms. Sokolov had promised the class they would learn to make a flat page look like a real street, and Emilia had been waiting for this lesson since September. London leaned over from the next table, already sharpening three pencils at once like she was preparing for surgery.

"Start with your vanishing point," Ms. Sokolov said, walking between the tables. "One dot. Then draw your orthogonals first." She tapped the air above Melody's paper and moved on without another word.

Emilia froze, pencil hovering. Orthogonals. She had written the word in her sketchbook that morning, circled it twice, and still had no idea what it meant. Melody raised her hand, but Ms. Sokolov was already across the room helping someone tape down a curling corner. The class rule was that a question could only go to the teacher twice per period, and Emilia had already used one asking whether the horizon line had to be straight. She needed to be objective about this, not just guess and waste her second question.

She looked at the example sketch Ms. Sokolov had pinned to the board. A street ran back toward a single dot, and faint pencil lines still showed beneath the ink. Slowly, Emilia traced them with her eyes. The road edges, the curbs, even the rooflines of the buildings on both sides, every one of them slanted toward that same dot. They weren't random. They were the bones of the whole picture, the lines that ran back toward the vanishing point. "Those are the orthogonals," she whispered, and felt like she'd found a hidden door. She drew her dot, then ran four lines toward it from the corners of her page, light as breath. The street appeared on her paper like it had been waiting there all along.

Then came the twist. Melody slid her own drawing over, grinning, and Emilia saw that Melody had put her vanishing point dead center, so the street ran straight and flat, like a road sitting on the equator instead of curving through a real town. "Yours looks alive," Melody said. "Mine looks like a diagram." Emilia tilted Melody's paper, then grabbed her eraser. She could fix this. She regulated her breathing, the way she did before a free throw, and moved the dot off to the left with one careful nudge.

"Now redraw your road edges," Emilia said, tapping the paper. "Curbs, rooflines, all of it, back to the new dot."

Melody's pencil was already moving.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Blushing happens when blood vessels in the face widen and let more blood flow near the skin.
story:
Piper got to the coffee shop ten minutes early, which she decided was the correct amount of early: enough to choose the good table by the window, not so much that she looked like she had been waiting since breakfast. The radiator under the window clicked and hissed, baking the air until the whole corner of the room felt as arid as a desert. She set her water glass in front of her like a prop, then moved it, then moved it back.

Liam arrived at exactly four o'clock, held up a thumb, and got in line for the counter. He came back with two hot chocolates, one for her, and said, "I guessed whipped cream. If that's wrong, the date is cancelled." She laughed, which was a good sign, and then she made a joke about the radiator being a dragon, and he laughed too, a real snorting laugh, and she felt her face go hot.

She knew what it was. She had read it in a library book about the body that nobody had ever borrowed before her: blushing happens when blood vessels in the face widen and let more blood flow near the skin. The warmth she felt was that extra blood doing its thing, right there under her skin, announcing itself to the entire coffee shop. She put her hands over her cheeks, which was like locking the barn after the horse had already ordered a latte.

In the bathroom she ran cold water over her wrists. If widened vessels meant more blood near the skin, then cold ought to work the other way, tightening things up. She held her wet wrists to her cheeks like two fish and stared at herself in the mirror. The red faded, slowly, the way a stain gives up. "Okay," she told the mirror. "Okay."

Genesis was at the sink, drying her hands. "Are you sick?" she asked. "Because if you have an infection, I'm standing very far from you."

"It's not an infection," Piper said. "It's just blushing."

"From what?"

"From a date. Table by the window. Don't look."

Genesis looked immediately and at length. Then she came back and said, "He's stacking whipped cream on his spoon like a tiny tower. I approve." When Piper sat down, Liam slid his whipped cream tower across the table to her.

"It collapsed," he said. "Like all towers."

She felt her face go warm again, and this time she just let it. "Your turn to blush," she said. "Tell me a joke and I'll laugh really hard at it, and we'll see if we can replicate the experiment."

"Replicate the experiment," Liam repeated, grinning. "On our first date."

"Only date," she said, "that comes with a control group," and she pointed her spoon at his cheeks, waiting for pink.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters" can push readers toward opposite opinions.
story:
Sofia wanted the last spot on the morning announcements crew, and so did Arjun. Ms. Bighorn said they would have to negotiate between themselves before Friday, which meant Sofia needed something impressive to trade or to show.

For her social studies project, she had picked two articles about the same downtown march. She spread them on the library table after school, with Arjun across from her and Adelie beside him, eating crackers. One headline said "Thousands of Protesters Fill Main Street." The other said "Rioters Disrupt Downtown." Sofia read both stories twice and frowned. The details matched almost exactly: the same street, the same crowd size, the same broken window near the end.

"That's weird," she said. "Same event. Completely different feeling."

Adelie leaned over. "The second one made me picture people smashing things. The first one made me picture people holding signs."

Arjun pointed at the words. "Protesters. Rioters. That's the whole difference. Loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd protesters or rioters can push readers toward opposite opinions." He shrugged. "My brother talks about this stuff at dinner."

Sofia tested it. She copied both headlines onto slips of paper, swapped the words, and slid them across the table to Adelie without saying which was original. "React to each one. Fast." Adelie read "Thousands of Rioters Fill Main Street" and said it sounded scary, like a curfew kind of thing. Then she read "Protesters Disrupt Downtown" and said it sounded annoying but basically normal. Same facts, opposite reactions, both times. Sofia wrote the results in her notebook with a pencil that was running out of voltage in its little electric sharpener, so the letters came out gray and streaky.

For her presentation, she made a versatile display board, one side for each headline, with the matching photos hidden behind flaps. When she lifted the flaps at the same moment, the class saw identical images of the same intersection. Ms. Bighorn stopped writing in her grade book and looked at the board for a long moment. "Where did you find the second article?" she asked. Sofia told her, and Ms. Bighorn wrote something down without explaining it.

After class, Arjun caught up with her in the hallway. "That was good," he said. "Trade you. You can have the announcements spot if I get to co-present the project at the district fair." Sofia thought about the fair, the microphone, the audience of judges, and how a headline could tilt a whole room before anyone read a single sentence. She stuck out her hand. "Deal," she said. "But you're carrying the board."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: 2 is the only even prime number, because every larger even number can be divided evenly by 2.
story:
The computer lab at Camp Windrow smelled like pine from the open window and warm keyboards from twenty laptops running at once. Florence sat in the back row with her screen tilted away from Randy, not because she was hiding anything, but because she wanted to type her program herself. Their counselor had given them the task that morning: write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime. Florence had a plan, and she wanted to follow it without anyone leaning over her shoulder.

Her plan was simple. If a number can be divided evenly by two, it is not prime, so her loop would check every number from two upward and flag the ones that divided evenly. She typed it out, and when she ran it the first time it asked for a number just the way it was supposed to. That felt like a small victory, so she allowed herself a grin before testing further.

Then the trouble started. She entered seven, and the program said prime. She entered nine, and it said not prime. So far so good. But when she entered two, the screen said not prime, which was wrong, because two was the very first prime number she had ever memorized back in fourth grade. "Oh, come on," she muttered. Randy looked over. "What did you violate this time?" he asked. "Some law of mathematics, apparently."

Ms. Wilson walked past and glanced at the screen, but she only said, "Test a few more numbers and see what they have in common," and moved on, which was her way of making the campers do their own detective work. Florence tried four, six, eight and ten, and every single one came back not prime. Then she tried three, five and seven, and those were prime. The pattern was gradual at first, like fog clearing, but then it snapped into focus: two was the only even prime number, because every larger even number could be divided evenly by two. Her loop was punishing two for being even, and that was the bug.

She fixed it by making her program treat two as a special case before the loop ever started. When she ran it again, the screen said two was prime, and she sat back so fast her chair squeaked. Randy leaned over. "So what was it?" "Two," she said. "My own program was the jury, and it convicted the wrong number." He laughed and pulled his chair closer, copying her special case into his own code while Florence watched the cursor blink on her screen, waiting for the next test.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift after spellings had started to become fixed, which is a major reason English spelling often doesn't match pronunciation.
story:
Riley stood backstage at the community center gym with a stack of index cards shaking slightly in his hand. In five minutes the regional spelling bee would begin, and he was stuck on the same word he had missed at practice for a week: "bite." He kept wanting to write B-I-T, because that was how the short word sounded in his head. The silent e felt like a trap set on purpose. Octavia, waiting beside him in line, leaned over. "You're mouthing it again," she whispered. "You looked like a goldfish."

"I can't figure out why there's an extra letter nobody says," Riley whispered back. "There has to be a reason." He refused to abandon the question, even though his coach had told him to just memorize and stop wondering. Before the bee, Eleanor had slipped a folded note into his jacket pocket, saying it might help with his vowel problem. He hadn't had a chance to read it yet. He ducked behind the bleachers and opened it.

"Riley," the note read, "I looked it up after you complained on Tuesday. Between about 1400 and 1700, English vowel sounds changed in the Great Vowel Shift, and that happened after spellings had started to become fixed. That's the big reason English spelling often doesn't match how we say things. So 'bite' isn't a trick. The letters just stopped moving before the sounds did. Good luck. Eleanor."

Riley read it twice, and something clicked. The e in "bite" was like a fossil, a mark left behind by an older version of the word. The spelling was a photograph of how people used to talk. It wasn't random, and that made it easier to remember. He folded the note, slid it into his pocket, and walked back to the line just as Ms. Nakamura, the bee coordinator, called his name. He crossed the gym floor to the microphone, and the judges conferred and then were unanimous on his first word: "height."

"H-E-I-G-H-T," Riley said slowly. In his mind he pictured the word as an old artifact, sounds that had drifted while the letters stayed put. The judges nodded, and the announcer's voice rang out over the gym. "That is correct." Riley grinned and looked toward the bleachers, where Octavia gave him a thumbs up, and he whispered, "Two hundred years of history says I can spell."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: An opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion, but it is a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons.
story:
Alexandre had one goal for his lunch break in the library: convince Ms. Ramos, who ran the student council, that the school needed a petition for a crosswalk on Maple Street. He had his argument ready. "It's dangerous," he announced, dropping his books on the table where Maddison and Braydon were already sitting. "Everyone says so."

Maddison looked up from her notebook. "Everyone says the cafeteria pizza is dangerous too." Braydon snorted so hard he knocked over his pencil cup. Ms. Ramos, shelving books three feet away, gave them a look that seemed to govern the whole room, because both boys straightened up at once.

"That's different," Alexandre said. "The pizza is just gross. That's an opinion." He paused, because the word felt slippery. "I mean, saying the street is dangerous is also an opinion, isn't it?"

"That's where you're wrong," Maddison said, and turned her notebook around. She had drawn a grid with tally marks filling four rows. "I stood at the corner after school for three days. Twelve times a car screeched or swerved while somebody was crossing. I counted. Twelve near-misses." Braydon leaned over and whistled. Alexandre read the numbers twice, and something clicked into place, like when his grandfather's clock prescription finally arrived in the mail and the old gears began turning again with a soft, luminous glow behind the glass. The count was real. He could picture each mark becoming a screech of tires.

"So your opinion has evidence," Alexandre said slowly. "It's still an opinion, but it's a more convincing one than mine, because I gave no reasons." Maddison nodded. "Exactly. Try it again."

Alexandre stood, took a breath, and spoke as if Ms. Ramos were actually listening instead of pretending to alphabetize biographies. "I think the city should build a crosswalk on Maple Street. Twelve near-misses in three days is my reason." He heard Braydon mutter "ooh, data boy" under his breath, which was annoying but also kind of great.

"Better," said Ms. Ramos, sliding a biography of Marie Curie onto the shelf. "But I have a question for you, data boy." She turned around, holding a city map. "If your numbers came from the wrong corner, would they still be evidence?" Alexandre felt his stomach drop. He looked at Maddison, whose tally sheet suddenly seemed very small. "Which corner did you watch?" he asked. "The one by the bakery," she said. Braydon pointed at the map and grinned. "The bakery's on Oak Street."

Alexandre stared at the map for a long moment, then grabbed a fresh pencil. "Same method," he said. "Right corner. Tomorrow, three o'clock." Maddison was already drawing a new grid.

activity: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
knowledge_domain: to solve linear equations with one variable by doing the same operation to both sides
fact: Like terms can be combined before solving, so 2x + 3x becomes 5x, but 2x and 3 cannot be combined because one has a variable and one does not.
story:
The corner store smelled like oranges and floor cleaner, and Ivy had claimed the stool by the window because it was the only place in the neighborhood where she could think without her little brother asking to play. She spread her math homework across the counter space Mr. Chea let her use, a worksheet on solving equations, and stared at the first problem until the letters blurred. Across the aisle, Jessy was reading the label on a can of tropical fruit salad and arguing with a boy from their grade about whether pineapple belonged in the same category as mango.

The boy, whose grandmother owned the store, had his own math on a scrap of paper. He wrote fast, tongue between his teeth, and then shoved the paper toward his grandmother at the register. "Done. 2x plus 3, that's 5x."

His grandmother, a small woman with reading glasses on a chain, picked up the paper and frowned at it. Then she turned to the shelf and started restacking cans, leaving him standing there. "My grandma was a teacher," the boy said to Ivy, half proud and half embarrassed. "She won't just tell me. She asked me what the x stands for and then went back to work."

Ivy looked at her own worksheet. She had done the same thing two problems ago, squashing 2x + 3x into 5x with no trouble, and then hesitating when she hit 2x + 3. She pulled her pencil down the margin and wrote both expressions side by side. Two x's and three more x's, that was five x's, like putting four cans of tropical fruit with one more can and getting five cans. But 2x and 3 were not the same kind of thing at all. You could not add cans of soup to bags of rice and call it all soup.

"I think I get it," she said slowly. "They're like terms, the x ones. The plain numbers are a different kind."

"Like sorting," Jessy called over, not looking up from her can. "You categorize things before you count them."

The boy erased his 5x. He tapped his pencil, wrote 2x + 3 again, and left it alone. Then he flipped his paper toward his grandmother once more, and this time she looked at it for a long moment and gave him a single nod before turning back to the customer at the register.

Ivy went back to her first problem, which had 4x + 7 + x on the left side of the equals sign. She combined the x's into 5x, wrote it down, and then did the same thing to both sides, subtracting seven from each. The equation shrank under her pencil until x stood alone, equal to a number she could actually check. Outside, a delivery truck pulled up with crates of winter apples, a small piece of agriculture rumbling to the curb, and Mr. Chea went out to meet it.

"Twenty minutes till closing," the grandmother called.

"Then I have twenty minutes," Ivy said, and turned the page.

activity: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
knowledge_domain: customs such as greetings, gift-giving and table manners that differ between cultures and households
fact: In Japan, bowing is a common greeting, and generally the longer and deeper the bow, the more respect it shows.
story:
The reception line moved slowly, and Sara's gift bag sweated in her hands. Julianne had said her family's weddings ran long on ceremony, but Sara hadn't expected the bride's grandparents to stand at the front greeting every single guest, one by one.

"That's Obaachan and Ojiichan," Julianne whispered. "They came over from Kyoto last week. You'll bow."

"Bow how?" Sara asked, but the line was already pushing her forward, and Julianne got swallowed by a hug from a great-aunt.

Sara watched. That was the only thing she could do, so she did it properly, counting in her head like she was running an experiment. A cousin shook the grandmother's hand and gave a small nod, barely a dip of the chin. The grandmother nodded back the same size, quick and light. Then an older man in a grey suit stepped up, pressed his gift forward with both hands, and bent from the waist in a slow, deep bow that held for what felt like ten seconds. The grandfather answered with a bow just as long and just as deep. Then a teenage boy, clearly in a hurry, mumbled something and ducked his head about an inch, and the grandmother's returning nod was small and fast, almost clipped.

So there was a pattern. A shallow, quick bow got a shallow, quick bow, and a long, deep one got a long, deep one. The reasoning came together in Sara's head: the bow was like a mirror, but it was also like a measurement. The longer and deeper it was, the more respect it carried, which meant she had to decide, right now, how much respect she wanted to show. Too shallow and she'd look like the hurried boy. Too deep and she might look like she was pretending to be somebody important.

Her turn. She handed the gift with both hands, the way the man in the grey suit had done, because that part she could verify had worked. Then she bent from the waist, slow and steady, and held it, counting to five, terrified she'd misjudged.

When she straightened, Obaachan was smiling. She bowed back, long and deep, and said something to Julianne's mother, who laughed and translated: "She says you have better manners than half the relatives."

At the dinner table, Sara sat between Hayden and the teenage boy, who turned out to be named Ken and to be the bride's cousin, not rude at all, just jet-lagged and lethargic from the flight. He showed her how to hold her chopsticks to take food from the shared plates, and she showed him the trick of balancing a dinner roll on the butter knife, which made him laugh so hard he had to put his water glass down.

Later, when the dancing started, Obaachan caught Sara's eye across the room and gave her one more small, careful bow. Sara bowed back, exactly the same size, and held it until she heard the old woman laugh.

activity: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
knowledge_domain: to write a short story with correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax
fact: When a dialogue tag follows a spoken sentence, the sentence ends with a comma inside the quotation marks instead of a period, as in "I'm ready," she said.
story:
The porch boards at his grandfather's house still smelled of cedar oil, and Edouard sat cross-legged on them with his notebook, listening to the screen door bang behind Kallie. She had ridden her bike over with a red pen stuck behind her ear and a claim that made his stomach drop. "I marked every period before 'she said' in your draft," she said, flipping to the last page. "Every single one. It's an infection of periods, Edouard. It spread through the whole story."

He took the notebook and saw the red circles, twenty-three of them, crowding his dialogue like ants at a picnic. His story was due at tomorrow's writing club meeting, and Ms. Sun had said the assignment needed correctly punctuated dialogue and a clear climax. He had spent all week on the climax, a scene where two brothers argue during a storm on a lake, but he had not thought once about commas.

Kallie leaned against the porch rail and munched a stolen plum from the bowl by the door. She was not going to tell him the rule straight out; that was her way, and it had hindered him more than once, though it also made him remember things better. She pointed at his first line, where he had written: "I'm not turning back." she said. Then she wrote her own sentence on the corner of the page: "I'm ready," she said. "Compare them," Kallie said. "Look what happens when the tag comes after."

Edouard stared at the two sentences until his eyes ached. In hers, the spoken part ended with a comma sitting inside the quotation marks, not a period at all, and then "she said" followed in lowercase. The speaker's sentence flowed into the tag like a river into a wider river. He thought about last year, when he had guessed on every punctuation question and earned his worst grade of middle school. He had promised himself he would stop guessing. So now he tested it, being systematic the way his grandfather was when he sorted screws into jars: he wrote five new lines of dialogue, each with the tag after the spoken words, each ending with the comma inside the quotation marks. Kallie checked them one by one and shrugged, which meant they were right.

"Wait," he said suddenly. "Then the period only goes there when nothing follows. When the tag comes after, it's the comma instead." Kallie grinned and split the last plum in half with her thumb, offering him the bigger piece. Somewhere in the garden his grandfather's sprinkler ticked on, and Edouard picked up his pen and went back to the brothers on the lake, fixing the first red circle on the page. "I'm not turning back," he wrote, "she said." Then he crossed it out, and wrote it again the right way.
